result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.bipartite_vertex_cover()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a minimum vertex cover of a bipartite graph (König's theorem). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L44142-L44214){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.bipartite_vertex_cover(top_nodes=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Bipartite vertex cover](/assets/graphs/bipartite-vertex-cover.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A bipartite graph with A, B, C on the top row and D, E on the bottom row, and edges A–D, A–E, B–E, and C–E. The minimum vertex cover is A and E, in the accent color: every edge touches one of them. A maximum matching, A–D and B–E in a second color, has the same size, as König's theorem says. The card shows the cover [A, E] and the matching, both of size 2." width="100%"} A vertex cover is a set of nodes that touches every edge. Finding the smallest one is hard in general, but on bipartite graphs it is easy: by König's theorem its size equals the size of a maximum matching, and it can be read off from one. Vertex covers answer questions like "which fewest people must be interviewed so that every reported interaction involves one of them?", or "which fewest checkpoints monitor every road between two districts?". The sides are found by 2-coloring the graph (ignoring edge direction) unless they are given with `top_nodes=`. Any valid split gives a minimum cover, though possibly a different one. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [top_nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional list of the nodes on one side (IDs or labels); all other nodes form the other side. If `None` (default), the sides are found automatically. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node IDs of a minimum vertex cover, in ascending order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite, or `top_nodes=` leaves an edge within one side. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} After computing a maximum matching $M$ with Hopcroft-Karp, the method collects the set $Z$ of nodes reachable from unmatched top nodes along alternating paths (non-matching edges from top to bottom, matching edges back up). The cover is the top nodes outside $Z$ plus the bottom nodes inside it, which has exactly $|M|$ nodes (König 1931). The total time is $O(E \sqrt{V})$. For non-bipartite graphs, see `min_weighted_vertex_cover()` for a 2-approximation. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every edge of this small bipartite graph touches A or E, so two nodes suffice, matching the size of a maximum matching: ::: {#ca36ae08 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) g.add_edges([("A", "D"), ("A", "E"), ("B", "E"), ("C", "E")]) cover = g.bipartite_vertex_cover() [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in cover], len(g.bipartite_maximum_matching()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['A', 'E'], 2) ``` ::: ::: `is_vertex_cover()` confirms that every edge is touched: ::: {#78aa4cc0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.is_vertex_cover(cover) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
